slides.label: Title
slides.notes: Open by naming the shift in this chapter: the Einstein equation is no longer only a curvature condition to solve, but a machine that filters possible topologies. The lecture follows the source span from low-dimensional cases through group and spin obstructions, then ends with the Cheeger-Gromoll splitting theorem as a structural statement about nonnegative Ricci curvature. Emphasize that the diagrams are original teaching models, not copied source figures.

slides.label: Roadmap
slides.notes: Use the roadmap as a dependency check rather than as a list of topics. The same equation feeds several kinds of topology: classification in small dimensions, restrictions on fundamental groups, spinorial vanishing arguments, and global splitting. Ask students to listen for which hypothesis opens each gate, because changing the sign of lambda or removing compactness changes the conclusion.

slides.label: Dimension Two
slides.notes: The surface case is the chapter in miniature. Because Ricci is just Gaussian curvature times the metric, the Einstein condition says the curvature is constant and Gauss-Bonnet immediately ties the sign to Euler characteristic. This is a good place to warn that the simplicity is special to dimension two; higher dimensions retain much more curvature information outside Ricci.

slides.label: Dimension Three
slides.notes: In dimension three there is no Weyl curvature, so the Ricci tensor determines the full curvature tensor. That means the Einstein equation is much stronger than it first looks: it gives constant sectional curvature rather than merely constant Ricci in averaged directions. The topological consequences are therefore tied to space-form geometry and to how a group can act on the corresponding model space.

slides.label: Dimension Four
slides.notes: Move slowly here because this is the hinge between tensor geometry and topology. In four dimensions, the Einstein condition kills the traceless Ricci block but leaves the Weyl blocks alive. Characteristic numbers can be expressed through curvature integrals, so an Einstein metric must make analytic curvature data compatible with topological quantities such as Euler characteristic and signature.

slides.label: Hitchin Thorpe
slides.notes: Present the inequality as a necessary gate, not as a classification theorem. The proof idea is that Chern-Weil formulas express topological invariants through curvature, and the Einstein condition simplifies the integrands enough to force a sign inequality. The visual cone helps students distinguish an obstruction from an existence result: the allowed region still contains many manifolds whose Einstein question remains hard.

slides.label: Fundamental Group
slides.notes: This slide organizes several group statements by the sign of the Einstein constant. Positive Ricci curvature is restrictive because comparison geometry supplies diameter and compactness consequences; Ricci-flat geometry is more delicate because flat factors can appear after passing to covers. Negative Ricci curvature does not impose the same finiteness pattern, so examples and obstructions must be read with the sign visible.

slides.label: Bochner Mechanism
slides.notes: Introduce Bochner reasoning as a reusable proof shape. The argument does not inspect topology directly; it shows that a harmonic or parallel object must vanish, and then translates that vanishing into a topological statement. This prepares the spinorial obstruction slide, where the relevant object is a spinor rather than a 1-form.

slides.label: Cover Geometry
slides.notes: The universal cover is the natural stage for fundamental group arguments. The lifted metric preserves the curvature condition, while the group appears as isometries of the cover. This lets the proof translate between geometry of geodesics and algebra of deck transformations, which is exactly the translation needed for splitting and finiteness results.

slides.label: Spin Obstruction
slides.notes: Frame spin geometry as an additional detector, not as a replacement for curvature comparison. The Dirac operator has an analytic square, while its index is topological, so the same object is pulled in two directions. For positive Einstein constant, scalar curvature is positive, and that positivity can contradict a nonzero index prediction.

slides.label: Scalar Sign
slides.notes: Pause on sign because it controls which arguments are legal. A theorem proved with positive scalar curvature cannot simply be carried into the Ricci-flat or negative case. This slide is a practical reading checklist: before applying Myers, Bochner, or a spinorial vanishing argument, first identify the sign of the Einstein constant and the compactness assumptions.

slides.label: Cheeger Gromoll
slides.notes: The splitting theorem should be read as geometry discovering an algebraic product. A line is a globally minimizing geodesic in both directions, and nonnegative Ricci curvature prevents the manifold from bending around it in an arbitrary way. In the Ricci-flat Einstein case, this theorem explains why Euclidean factors and virtually abelian pieces of the fundamental group naturally appear.

slides.label: Topology Dashboard
slides.notes: Treat the dashboard as the lecture's practical summary. Students should not memorize all obstructions as if they had the same hypotheses; each one requires different input data. A mature reading of the chapter means matching the manifold at hand to the correct test before making a claim about existence or nonexistence.

slides.label: Worked Sorting
slides.notes: Run this slide actively rather than as a passive list. For each candidate, ask students to name the first theorem they would try and one hypothesis they still need to verify. The aim is to build the habit of sorting obstructions by input data, which is more reliable than reacting to keywords such as spin, group, or four-manifold.

slides.label: Learner Lab
slides.notes: Connect the deck back to the assigned notebook. The experiments do not prove the theorems, but they make the logical structure inspectable: choose data, compute or mark an invariant, pass it through a gate, and explain the outcome. Encourage students to record failure cases because an obstruction is most memorable when they can see exactly which assumption breaks.

slides.label: Recap
slides.notes: Close by returning to the chapter's central promise: Einstein geometry can rule topology in or out before one solves a metric equation. The low-dimensional cases show rigidity, the four-dimensional case shows characteristic-number obstructions, and the group and spin sections show how analysis detects topology indirectly. The takeaway is not a single classification, but a toolkit for asking which topological gate an Einstein metric must pass.
